title: Erdős #124 — The Strong Version Excluding the Power d^0 = 1

problemStatement.formal: Given integers d_1, \ldots, d_k \ge 2, let S = \{\, d_i^{\,e} : 1 \le i \le k,\; e \ge 1 \,\} be the set of their powers with the exponent e = 0 (the value 1) excluded. For which tuples (d_1, \ldots, d_k) is S complete, i.e. every sufficiently large n \in \mathbb{N} a subset sum of S? Equivalently, for which (d_1, \ldots, d_k) can every large n be written as n = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i where each a_i uses only digits 0 and 1 in base d_i and has no constant term \varepsilon_{i,0}? In particular, does \sum_{i=1}^{k} \tfrac{1}{d_i - 1} \ge 1 still suffice once d_i^0 = 1 is forbidden, or must it be paired with \gcd(d_1,\ldots,d_k) = 1?
problemStatement.plain: The solved weak version of Erdős #124 lets every number be written as a sum where each summand uses only 0/1 digits in some base d_i, and it allows the digit-value 1 = d_i^0. The strong version forbids that value 1, leaving only the powers d_i, d_i^2, d_i^3, .... The open question is to determine exactly which tuples (d_1, ..., d_k) still make the resulting set of powers complete — able to represent all sufficiently large integers as subset sums — when the anchoring value 1 is removed.
whyMatters: Completes the historical record of Erdős #124: the celebrated AI solution (Harmonic Aristotle, 2025) resolved only the weak form; the strong reformulation excluding d^0 = 1 remains open.
Sharpens the theory of complete sequences by pinning down the exact threshold, and tests whether Brown's-criterion machinery survives the loss of the anchoring value 1 that its base case relies on.

knownResults: Erdős #124 weak version (with d^0 = 1 allowed) solved by Harmonic Aristotle (2025), formalized as erdos-124-complete-sequences.
Brown's criterion: a non-decreasing sequence with u_1 = 1 is complete iff u_{n+1} <= 1 + sum_{j<=n} u_j.
Cassels (1960): classical completeness criteria for subset sums of a fixed set of positive integers.
references: Burr, Erdős, Graham, Li, 'Complete sequences of sets of integer powers', Acta Arithmetica 77 (1996), 133-138.
Cassels, 'On the representation of integers as sums of distinct summands from a fixed set', Acta Sci. Math. Szeged 21 (1960), 111-124.
